performers: San Francisco Symphony Orchestra, Pierre Monteux; Naoum Blinder, violin
intro: Scheherazade’s violin introduces a bassoon with a tale of its own. Its winding B-minor melody passes to the oboe and strings, while brass fanfares keep interrupting.

sections.label: A · Bassoon over muted double basses
sections.mNote: Four double basses hold the floor beneath the solo

sections.label: B · Brass fanfares interrupt
sections.mNote: Short calls replace the long woodwind phrases

sections.label: Link · Clarinet and plucked strings
sections.mNote: A free clarinet solo crosses softly repeated string chords

sections.label: Dev · The brass march grows
sections.mNote: Piccolo and percussion join the orchestral march

sections.label: A′ · The bassoon speaks again
sections.mNote: A bassoon cadenza recalls the opening melody

sections.label: A″ · The tune fills the orchestra
sections.mNote: Winds and strings enlarge the bassoon’s melody

sections.label: Coda · Wind phrases, then B major
sections.mNote: The final Animato drives towards the major chord

cues.title: The violin returns
cues.text: The solo violin begins another winding recitative over harp chords. Scheherazade’s voice is familiar from the first movement. Her cadenza slows before a quite different soloist takes over.
cues.evidence: Full score, second movement, printed pp. 24–25: Lento, Recitativo, violin cadenza and ritardando before the bassoon. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bassoon and four double basses
cues.text: A bassoon begins in B minor, dolce ed espressivo — sweetly and expressively. Four muted double basses hold a quiet foundation beneath it. The tune mixes little dancing figures with longer notes, as though its teller keeps stopping to remember a detail.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 25: Andantino, bassoon marked Capriccioso, quasi recitando and dolce ed espressivo; four solo double basses, con sordino. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A violinist who taught Stern
cues.text: The solo violin is Naoum Blinder, concertmaster of the San Francisco Symphony. He reaches the United States in 1928 with the banker Felix Warburg’s sponsorship and teaches many violinists, Isaac Stern among them.
cues.evidence: Jewish Telegraphic Agency obituary of Naoum Blinder: former concertmaster of the San Francisco Symphony, teacher of Isaac Stern, in the United States from 1928 under Felix Warburg’s sponsorship. https://www.jta.org/archive/naoum-blinder-teacher-of-many-ranking-musicians-dies-in-san-francisco

cues.title: The tune in new colours
cues.text: The bassoon’s tune returns again and again in new colours. Strings shimmer in tremolo, a thrumming accompaniment turns beneath it, and sharper sounds prick the texture.
cues.evidence: Paul Serotsky describes the movement as a kaleidoscope of variations with string tremolandos, thrummings and pricking textures. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The professor teaches himself
cues.text: In 1871 Rimsky-Korsakov accepts a professorship at the Saint Petersburg Conservatory. He is twenty-seven. Alongside teaching, he sets about learning the harmony and counterpoint his own training has left out.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard gives the appointment and age; Paul Serotsky describes the subsequent self-education. https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade-last-movement ; https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm

cues.title: The brass breaks in
cues.text: The long melody meets short, fierce brass calls. The new idea grows out of the Sultan’s phrase from the first movement. Horns, trumpets and trombones turn it into a march.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 30–31; Serotsky identifies the central idea’s relation to the Sultan’s motto and its development into a march. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Not the Sultan
cues.text: The unison phrase that opened the suite for the stern Sultan returns in this movement’s brass. Rimsky-Korsakov says it serves here as musical material alone: in the Kalender’s tale, “there cannot, however, be any mention of Sultan Shakhriar.”
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life, translated by Judah A. Joffe, second edition, pp. 247–248. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf

cues.title: Clarinet over plucked strings
cues.text: A clarinet stretches the tune into a free solo. The strings pluck repeated chords beneath it, quickening and slowing with the soloist. The score asks the clarinet to begin lento, lungo — slowly, at length — before accelerating.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 32, rehearsal F: Moderato assai, Recitativo; clarinet ad libitum, lento lungo, accelerando; strings pizzicato and colla parte. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A fanfare that sails on
cues.text: The sharp fanfare for muted trumpet and trombone first sounds in this movement. Rimsky-Korsakov notes that it returns in the finale “in the delineation of the wrecking ship”, though that episode has no connection with the Kalender’s tale.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life, translated by Judah A. Joffe, second edition, pp. 247–248. A muted trumpet (con sord.) begins the fanfare before rehearsal E in the full score, printed p. 30. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf ; https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf

cues.title: The bassoon’s second tale
cues.text: The bassoon returns in a cadenza, answering the earlier clarinet solo. Its familiar tune opens the movement’s last large section. The same little figures now have the brass march behind them.
cues.evidence: Paul Serotsky describes the two cadenzas, first clarinet and then bassoon, with the bassoon initiating the final section. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Towards the B-major chord
cues.text: Short woodwind phrases prepare the final rush. The last page is marked Animato: strings race beneath brass chords, with timpani reinforcing the bass. A sharp final chord brings the B-minor tale to a B-major end.
cues.evidence: Full score, closing pages, especially printed p. 53: Animato and final B-major chord. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The violin leaves a bassoon
transitions.to: A · Bassoon over muted double basses
transitions.how: The violin’s cadenza slows, marked ritardando assai. At Andantino, the bassoon begins its B-minor tune above four muted double basses. The violin’s high ending hangs briefly over the new, much lower voice.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 25, end of the violin cadenza and opening Andantino. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf

transitions.title: The Sultan’s phrase becomes a march
transitions.from: A · Bassoon over muted double basses
transitions.how: A figure first plucked by the low strings grows into brass fanfares. Its kinship with the Sultan’s motto links the interruption to the first movement. Horns, trumpets and trombones exchange short calls while the sustained woodwinds and strings support them.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 30–31; Serotsky describes the low-string origin and the Sultan-motto connection. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm

transitions.title: Plucked strings under a free clarinet
transitions.how: The orchestral chord stops at a fermata. At Moderato assai, a solo clarinet takes up a free recitative. The strings pluck short repeated chords, following the soloist’s slowing and acceleration. Their soft attacks leave the clarinet’s long notes exposed.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 32, rehearsal F: clarinet solo and pizzicato strings marked colla parte. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf

source.title: Rimsky-Korsakov, Scheherazade, II, full-score scan
source.locator: Printed pp. 24–26: violin, bassoon and oboe solos; pp. 30–32: brass march and clarinet recitative with pizzicato strings; pp. 48–53: final return and B-major ending.

timeline.note: The solo violin winds above harp chords.
The bassoon begins above four muted double basses; harp and the violin’s held ending sound at the join.
The oboe takes the tune, with bassoon, horn and strings beneath it.
The strings take up the bassoon’s tune, with woodwinds joining its phrases.
Horns, trumpets and trombones exchange short fanfares above sustained strings and winds.
The clarinet plays freely above repeated pizzicato chords in the strings.
Piccolo, brass, timpani, triangle and cymbals join the strings as the march grows.
The bassoon recalls the opening tune above quiet strings.
Winds and strings broaden the tune, reinforced by brass and percussion.
Short woodwind phrases emerge as the orchestral accompaniment thins.
At Animato, strings race beneath brass chords; timpani and cymbals reinforce the B-major ending.

composer.epithet: He became a professor before he could write counterpoint, then built Russian fairy-tale operas around an orchestra he knew instrument by instrument.
facts: Naval College, Saint Petersburg; composition with Balakirev and years of private study
Conservatory professor from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Fifteen operas, from The Maid of Pskov to The Golden Cockerel
composer.background:
Before he had seen the sea, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov rigged a toy brig and read letters from his older brother Voyin, a naval officer. Growing up in Tikhvin, he wanted a ship of his own. His father took him to the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856; piano lessons continued alongside his naval education. In 1861 his teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Mily Balakirev, who encouraged the seventeen-year-old cadet to begin a symphony.

The clipper Almaz carried him away in 1862 for a voyage lasting nearly three years. During a long stop in England he wrote the symphony’s slow movement without a piano, snatching a chance to try it at a restaurant. He posted the music to Balakirev and received encouragement with requests for changes. Farther out, he watched the Gulf Stream turn the ocean blue and saw flying fish and phosphorescence. Back in Russia, music reclaimed him; Balakirev conducted the completed First Symphony in December 1865.
